**Chapter 1 analysis**

The draft compresses well overall. Let me check specific passages:

- "Miss Baker's lips fluttered; she nodded at me almost imperceptibly, then tipped her head back again, balancing some invisible object on her chin." — The source introduced Baker as the *younger of the two*, a stranger to Nick. In the draft, Daisy's murmur giving Baker's surname was cut. However, looking carefully: the draft has Miss Baker remarking "You must know Gatsby" in a compressed passage, so Baker is named before this passage. Parseable.

- "Tom hovered restlessly. 'I've got a nice place here,' he said, his eyes flashing about." — Tom already said this on the porch earlier in the draft ("'I've got a nice place here,' he said, his eyes flashing about."). This is a repeated line — an artifact of compression duplicating Tom's speech. A reader would be confused by Tom making the identical remark twice in the same chapter with no new context. Testing against criteria: this is a structural seam — the second instance is dangling without the intervening scene (showing the interior, showing the garden sweep) that in the source separates the two moments. The second occurrence in the draft reads as if it triggers the move toward dinner, but it's identical to what was already said on the porch. **This is a genuine broken pivot** — the second "I've got a nice place here" appears to be a vestige of a cut transitional passage. A reader would be confused about why Tom is repeating himself word-for-word.

- "She gathered up her purchases and went haughtily in." — The source had Mrs. Wilson buying a dog, a magazine, cold cream, and perfume at the station. The authorized cuts list includes "Myrtle's spur-of-the-moment puppy purchase." So "her purchases" refers to the magazine, cold cream, and perfume that were also in that passage. But the draft skips all of that entirely — it goes straight from "So Tom and his girl and I went up together to New York" to "Presently we were in a slice of a white apartment-house." There is no mention of any purchases in the draft. The word "her purchases" has no antecedent in the draft.

**Chapter 2 analysis**

Throwing a regal homecoming glance around the neighbourhood, she gathered up her purchases and went haughtily in." — As noted, "her purchases" has no antecedent in the draft. The puppy purchase was an authorized cut, but the magazine/drugstore stop was not authorized for removal — it was incidental to the puppy scene. However, the authorized cut of the puppy purchase swept out the whole station-exit scene, including those purchases. This is a residue of the authorized cut. - "One of them leaned close to me and whispered: 'Neither of them can stand the person they're married to.'" — "One of them" refers to company that "commenced to arrive — her sister and some neighbours." This is vague but parseable as one of the visitors. The source made clear this was Catherine. Catherine is an authorized removal. So "one of them" is an authorized-cut seam. NOT a finding.

- "I gathered that it was really his wife that was keeping them apart: 'She's a Catholic, and they don't believe in divorce.'" — This follows the whispered exchange. The source had Catherine say this. Now it's reported as Nick's inference with a quote. This reads oddly but does parse. Not structurally broken.

- "'Why did you, Myrtle?' someone demanded. 'Nobody forced you to.'" — In the source, Catherine asks this. Catherine is an authorized removal. "Someone demanded" covers the attribution. The question and answer are both present. NOT a finding (authorized removal).

- "Taking my hat, I followed someone into the elevator." — The source has: "Taking my hat from the chandelier, I followed [Mr. McKee]." Mr. McKee is an authorized removal. The sentence parses. NOT a finding.

Now back to Chapter 1's doubled Tom line:

Draft passage 1 (on the porch): *"We talked for a few minutes on the sunny porch. 'I've got a nice place here,' he said, his eyes flashing about. He swept a broad flat hand across sunken gardens and roses and the snub-nosed motorboat that bumped the tide offshore."*

Draft passage 2 (after interior scene, before dinner): *"Tom hovered restlessly. 'I've got a nice place here,' he said, his eyes flashing about. He proposed we go out again; instead we moved toward the porch where four candles flickered on the table in the diminished wind."*

The source's second "I've got a nice place here" does NOT exist — the source has Tom say this only once, on the porch. The draft's compression of the hallway/living-room scene has accidentally duplicated Tom's porch line and inserted it mid-interior. A reader would be genuinely confused: Tom repeats verbatim a remark he just made, and then "proposes going out again" when the party never went inside (in the reader's understanding) because the transition was obscured. The "He proposed we go out again; instead we moved toward the porch" is also confusing — the reader has no clear sense they were inside, because the interior transition was compressed into a single paragraph beginning "We walked through a high hallway." This is a broken logical structure: the second Tom speech acts as a pivot toward dinner but its triggering context (being inside, needing to return outside) is unclear, and the verbatim repetition makes it read as an error.

Let me verify this clears the gate test: A competent reader with no source access reads Tom say "I've got a nice place here" with eyes flashing on the porch, then two paragraphs later reads Tom say the exact same words again with the same physical description, then "proposed going out again" when there's been no clear establishment that they went in. Yes — genuinely confused, not just less-ornamented.

This is a **broken_pivot**: the connective logic of the scene transition was cut, and Tom's second speech (which in the draft is identical to his first) now reads as unmotivated repetition without the scene-change context.
